title: Cornell faculty prepare no-confidence vote against administration over handling of alleged sexual assault case | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Members of the Cornell University Faculty Senate have introduced a resolution for a vote of no confidence against the university administration for its handling of the2024 alleged gang rape on campus, as calls for reform and accountability reverberate with hundreds of protesters gathering on campus.

The resolution was submitted to the university faculty committee Monday evening, according to Paul Ortiz, a professor of labor history at Cornell who is also a member of the Faculty Senate. The group will review the resolution and it will be put on the full Faculty Senate agenda for when the Senate meets on October 14, Ortiz said.

A vote of no confidence, meant to convey a group has lost faith in a leader or administration, would be a sign of serious dissatisfaction and put pressure on university leadership to take action. “The faculty have been approached by hundreds of students, alumni, staff who are demanding that we do something,” Ortiz told CNN.

CNN has reached out to Cornell for comment.

Frustrations with the administration were made clear Monday night during a rally on campus as students and community members chanted “shame” and “resign,” expressing raw anger at the officials they believe failed the woman known as Jane Doe when she initially made a report to campus police in 2024.

Some groups are also planning to host a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday “in solidarity with Jane Doe,” according to social media flyers for the event.

The lawsuit Doe filed last month against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity, seven fraternity members and others alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students. The ensuing fallout has raised questions about how the campus police investigation was handled, how the country district attorney made the decision not to file charges and whether the school’s internal investigation and ensuing actions went far enough.

The move comes just days after Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff,released a video statementpromising further review and answers for the community, saying Doe’s alleged experiences raise “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”

Kotlikoff said he supports the governor’s decision toturn the criminal investigation over to the New York Attorney Generaland welcomes an independent review by an outside law firm into Cornell’s handling of the 2024 case.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Taylor Galgano, Danya Gainor, Isa Mudannayake and Holly Yan contributed to this report.
